sections.h: Attempt 3: crtsh + dnsdumpster + hackertarget — real results

$ theHarvester -d radblok.co.za -b crtsh,dnsdumpster,hackertarget

[!] Missing API key for DNSDumpster.

mail.radblok.co.za:216.24.57.1

head: Source
Outcome
rows: **Skipped** — now requires an API key. Was free when documented in Entry 005. Policy changed.

blocks.text: One real finding: **`mail.radblok.co.za` resolves to `216.24.57.1`**. This subdomain was not in the whois record — it came from CT logs or hackertarget's passive DNS crawl. theHarvester found something that wasn't directly visible before.

head: Piece
What it means
rows: A subdomain — whoever set up the domain created a `mail` DNS record. Standard naming for a mail server.
The IP address that subdomain resolves to. Almost certainly xneelo's shared mail hosting — the same provider as the registrar and nameservers.
whois only shows nameservers and registrar. Subdomains and their IPs live in DNS records, not the whois record — which is why tools like theHarvester exist.

blocks.text: From a recon perspective: finding `mail.radblok.co.za` confirms there is mail infrastructure set up for the domain. Combined with the MX record (which `dig radblok.co.za MX` will show), this tells you where inbound email is handled. The IP `216.24.57.1` is the next thing to investigate — a reverse DNS lookup and a port scan would tell you what's running there.

blocks.label: kali — follow-up lookups
blocks.text:
# What subdomain does 216.24.57.1 reverse-resolve to?
$ dig -x 216.24.57.1 +short

# What MX record does radblok.co.za have?
$ dig radblok.co.za MX +short

# Does mail.radblok.co.za match what dig says directly?
$ dig mail.radblok.co.za A +short

For a target you don't own, `mail.*` is a high-value subdomain — mail servers often run older software, expose SMTP banners with version info, and are less aggressively patched than web servers. On your own domain, it's a reminder to check what's actually listening on port 25/587/993 at that IP.
DNSDumpster was listed in Entry 008 as a free no-API-key source. That was true when Entry 005 was written — it has since moved to a key-required model. To use it:

items: Register at dnsdumpster.com and get a free API key.
Add it to `/etc/theHarvester/api-keys.yaml` under the `dnsdumpster` key.
Re-run — theHarvester will pick it up automatically.

blocks.text: Several theHarvester sources have gone API-key-only over time as their providers tightened access. Always check the `[!] Missing API key` lines in output — they tell you which sources were silently skipped.

items: Confirmed `-b google` still broken — not worth trying again.
DNSDumpster now requires an API key — not free anymore, update api-keys.yaml if wanted.
**Real finding**: `mail.radblok.co.za:216.24.57.1` — a mail subdomain not visible in whois, found via CT logs / passive DNS.
This is what theHarvester is for: surfacing DNS records that exist but aren't advertised.
Next: `dig radblok.co.za MX`, `dig mail.radblok.co.za A`, and `dig -x 216.24.57.1` to follow up on the mail server finding.
